bracket: [Textbook error in this worked example, CORRECTED below rather than preserved, because a printed worked solution is a method a student copies. The book reverses equation (ii) to obtain (vi) but keeps its enthalpy NEGATIVE, at \(-3267.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); reversing a reaction must flip the sign. The defect is self-refuting on the book's own arithmetic: adding its printed (v) and (vi) as printed gives \(-3218.49 + (-3267.0) = -6485.49\), not the \(-48.51\) it goes on to print — while \(-3218.49 + 3267.0 = +48.51\) exactly, so the book evidently computed with \(+3267.0\) and then printed the sign wrong a second time on its final line. Corroborated independently by the book itself: Table 5.2 lists the standard enthalpy of formation of benzene(l) as \(+49.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Benzene is an endothermic compound, so a NEGATIVE \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) is not merely a slip of sign but the opposite chemical claim. Two further defects are left as printed because they change nothing: the reversed equation is still labelled \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) where \(-\Delta_C H^{\ominus}\) belongs, and the final line re-uses the label "(iv)", already used by equation (iv) above it.]

[Textbook errors in this worked example. TWO defects, treated differently on purpose. (1) THE UNIT IS CORRECTED. The printed line multiplies \(\text{R} = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) by a temperature and two dimensionless factors, so the result is JOULES per mole; the book prints \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), overstating the free-energy change by a factor of 1000. That is unambiguous and is fixed below. (2) THE VALUE IS LEFT AS PRINTED AND IS FLAGGED RATHER THAN CHANGED. Evaluating the book's own printed factors, \(8.314 \times 333 \times 2.303 \times 0.1239 = 790.0\), so the line does not give the \(763.8\) it prints. We cannot reconstruct which of the book's inputs it actually intended — no self-consistent reading of \(K_p\), \(T\) or \(\log K_p\) reproduces 763.8 — and inventing a correction would be worse than naming a defect, so the printed value stands. Expect the book's \(-763.8\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\) in any answer key; a derivation from the stated data gives about \(-790\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\).]

[Textbook error — THE QUESTION CONTRADICTS ITSELF, and which reading you take changes the answer. The prose introduces the reactant as \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(s)\) while the equation printed directly beneath it writes \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(g)\). The two readings give different \(\Delta n_g\) and therefore different answers, and BOTH are internally consistent: as a SOLID, \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 1.5 = +0.5\) and \(\Delta H = -741.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); as a GAS, \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 2.5 = -0.5\) and \(\Delta H = -743.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). The answer below takes the SOLID, for two reasons: it is what the question's own prose states, and cyanamide melts near \(44\,^\circ\text{C}\) so it is a solid at the stated \(298\,\text{K}\) — a bomb calorimeter is loaded with the solid. THE PRINTED ANSWER KEY TAKES THE GAS: it prints \(-743.939\,\text{kJ}\), which is reproduced to all six figures by \(-742.7 - 0.5(8.314\times10^{-3})(298)\). Both values are named here because an examiner following the book's key will expect \(-743.9\), and a student who answered \(-741.5\) from the printed prose is not wrong.]

[Textbook misprint in the option labels, affecting navigation rather than the answer.
